content: Condoms are manufactured from various materials, including latex, polyurethane, polyisoprene, lambskin, and nitrile. They function by creating a physical barrier that prevents sperm from entering the vagina, thereby reducing the risk of pregnancy. Additionally, condoms help prevent the transmission of infections present in semen, on the penis, or in the vagina, protecting both partners. The effectiveness of condoms depends on consistent and correct use. The risk of pregnancy or sexually transmitted infections (STIs) is highest when condoms are not used during every sexual encounter. Incorrect use, slippage, or breakage accounts for a small number of pregnancies or infections. For pregnancy prevention: With typical use, approximately 13 pregnancies occur per 100 women whose partners use male condoms during the first year. This means 87 out of 100 women will not become pregnant. With perfect use, about 2 pregnancies occur per 100 women during the first year. Fertility returns immediately after discontinuing condom use, with no delay. Regarding protection against HIV and other STIs: Male condoms, when used correctly and consistently during vaginal or anal sex, significantly reduce the risk of HIV transmission by 80–95%. They also reduce the risk of many other STIs, particularly those spread through discharge (e.g., HIV, gonorrhea, chlamydia) and skin-to-skin contact (e.g., herpes, human papillomavirus [HPV]). Latex male condoms are safe for all men
